adCopy: Every cat carries a map of home in her head. Last winter, I watched Hazel's start to go blank, one room at a time. First it was the laundry room. She'd stop in the doorway and stare, like she'd never been in there before. Then the upstairs bathroom. Then the hallway to her own water bowl. Then one night, she looked at me the same way. Our regular vet said she was just getting old. I asked for a referral anyway. The estimate was $1,140. Brain MRI, general anesthesia, one night of monitoring. For a 17-year-old cat who weighs 7 pounds. The receptionist slid the clipboard across the counter, and I picked up the pen. I was going to sign it. I want you to know that. I would have signed anything that might tell me why my cat had started looking at me like a stranger. Then the vet tech who'd been holding Hazel's carrier said, "I'll walk you out." In the parking lot, she set the carrier on the hood of my car and lowered her voice. "Can I be honest with you? The scan can rule out a tumor, and that's worth something. But if it's what we all think it is, you'll leave with the same advice you already got. She's old. Keep her comfortable." I asked what she meant. "There's nothing approved for this in cats," she said. "Not one thing. Has anyone even checked her blood pressure?" Nobody had. She glanced back at the clinic door like she'd said too much, and went inside. I didn't sign. I sat in the car with Hazel for twenty minutes, and one sentence kept going around in my head. Not one thing. I spent my whole career as a dental hygienist. I know what it sounds like when someone in scrubs tells you something they're not supposed to say out loud. So I went home and started reading. My name is Linda. I'm 61, retired now, and I live outside Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. I adopted Hazel, a tiny tortoiseshell, the spring my mother was diagnosed with dementia. For nine years Hazel sat on my lap while I learned what it looks like when someone you love forgets you. My mother would look at me, polite and blank, and ask the nurse who I was. So when Hazel started changing last winter, I recognized the look before anyone gave it a name. First she asked for breakfast fifteen minutes after breakfast. I caught myself saying out loud, "I did feed you, right?" Then she walked right past her litter box and peed beside it. Then the bathroom. The same bathroom she'd slept in on cold nights for seventeen years. I found her standing in the middle of the floor, crying, turning in a slow circle like the walls had moved. And then one Sunday she looked up at me from the bed. No purr. No chirp. Two full seconds of nothing in her eyes before something clicked and she put her head back down. Here's what I'd done about it, and what it cost. - Two senior blood panels: $898. Kidneys, liver, thyroid. "Great for her age." - A brain-support capsule from the clinic: $44 a month for three months. She gagged on it every single time. When I finally read the small print on the box, it was labeled for dogs. - A cheap cognition powder: $14. She sniffed her dinner, backed away, and skipped the meal. - Gabapentin "to settle her": $95 with the recheck. She stopped crying, and she stopped being Hazel. A ragdoll on my lap with her eyes half open. Every time, somebody said this might help. Every time, I paid, I waited, and she slipped a little further away. My brother had started asking, gently, whether it was "time." That week I did what I'd learned to do for my mother. I opened a folder. I printed things. I highlighted things. I searched "cat dementia treatment," then "senior cat forgets she ate," then "cat doesn't recognize me." The first thing I learned was that the tech was right. The Merck Veterinary Manual, the reference vets learn from, says plainly that "no drugs or diets are licensed to treat" this condition in cats. There is a brain drug for old dogs. It was approved in 1998. In the 28 years since, nothing has been approved for old cats. The best-known senior brain capsule in America is labeled for dogs. Another one the forums used to swear by has been discontinued. Then I learned what I should have been asking for all along. High blood pressure can make an old cat disoriented. A cat losing her sight or hearing can look exactly like a cat losing her mind. Thyroid trouble, arthritis and kidney disease can all look like dementia, and some of them can be fixed in weeks. In one large study of cats over 11, only about 1 in 4 had ever had their blood pressure measured. The next morning I called the clinic and asked for a blood pressure check and an eye exam. Both came back normal. So did her hearing. I was almost disappointed. I'd wanted it to be something they could fix. It wasn't. It was her brain. So I kept reading, and I found the part nobody had told me. Scientists aren't shrugging at old cats' brains. They're studying them. In 2025, a team at the University of Edinburgh looked inside the brains of old cats with dementia. They found amyloid, the same sticky protein found in human Alzheimer's, building up inside the connections between brain cells. And the brain's own clean-up cells were eating those connections away. Other researchers found the same tangles that show up in human Alzheimer's. A brain-scan study found that cat brains shrink with age in the same pattern ours do. A 15-year-old cat's brain has aged about as much as an 80-year-old person's. Professor Danièlle Gunn-Moore, one of the best-known feline researchers in the world, calls feline dementia "the perfect natural model for Alzheimer's." Read that again. Researchers use our cats' brains to understand human dementia. And on Hazel's paperwork, it said "geriatric." Even the official senior-cat guidelines written for vets admit that owners and veterinarians tend to blame this on "just being an old cat." That's when Hazel finally made sense to me. Every cat carries a map in her head. Where the bowl is. Where the box is. Which hallway leads to the bedroom. Whose face means home. The roads on that map are the connections between brain cells. As they wear away, she still walks the house, but the map has blank spots. That's why she forgets she just ate. In one study, 43% of cats with this condition cried for food after they'd already eaten. That's why she stares at walls. About half of them do. That's why she got lost in a bathroom she'd known for seventeen years. And that's why, for two seconds on a Sunday, the map hadn't filled in my face yet. She hadn't stopped loving me. Her map was fading. I'm not proud of it, but I was furious. I added it up on the back of an envelope. $1,139 in eight months. Kidneys, checked. Liver, checked. Thyroid, checked twice. Every test I paid for measured everything except the part of her that was disappearing. And the only thing anyone had given her for the behavior was a drug that switched her off. It made her quiet. It didn't help her find her way. Then the anger turned into a more useful question. If the map fades one connection at a time, waiting is the worst thing I can do. Researchers who tested a brain supplement in old cats found it helped the cats who were still sharper and did nothing for the most impaired ones. Hazel still had good hours. She was still in there. Whatever I was going to do, I had to do it while there was still a map to work with. The answer came from somewhere I didn't expect: a 340-year-old medical book. Around 1687, a Chinese physician named Chen Shiduo wrote about something his colleagues had lumped in with ordinary forgetfulness. He described old people who "forget recent events" and stay "at a loss" even when someone reminds them. Hazel, asking for breakfast fifteen minutes after breakfast. His tradition called the brain the "sea of marrow" and believed it drains with age. So he wrote a formula to replenish it, and he gave it a name I still can't read without tearing up. The "Supporting-the-Old Pill." Its largest ingredient was rehmannia root. Beside it was dang gui (angelica root) and, by most readings of the old text, astragalus. It wasn't a one-off. When researchers analyzed 236 dementia formulas from Chinese medical books spanning ten centuries, angelica and rehmannia were both among the ten most-used herbs. Modern labs have looked too. In naturally aged rats, a compound from rehmannia called catalpol improved memory and raised the proteins that build the connections between brain cells. The connections. The roads on the map. I'll be straight with you: those were rats. Nobody has studied these herbs for memory in cats. I knew that going in. Then I found a small company called Paw & Fam that had made a version for cats: Brain & Behavioral Serenity. It has rehmannia, dang gui and astragalus, three herbs from that 1687 formula, plus cultivated cordyceps mushroom. It answered every way the last eight months had failed her. The capsule she gagged on? This is a bacon-flavored liquid that goes in her dinner. The gabapentin that switched her off? This isn't a sedative. It's daily support for her brain, not an off switch. The "trust us"? They tested it in 40 cats for 90 days, with vet exams at the start and the end. No serious side effects, and the cats ate it mixed into their food from day one. They were also upfront that the cats in their test were no older than 16. Hazel is 17 and her kidney values are borderline, so I showed the label to my vet before the first drop. She said to go ahead and watch her stools that first week. Then I made a deal with myself. The guarantee was 90 days, so that was my deadline. If I couldn't see more of Hazel by then, I'd send it back, and I'd stop. The bottle came with a simple tracker called the Good Days Journal. It has six checks a day: found her bowl, used her box, came when called, purred or groomed, lost moments, staring spells. The same week, I followed the setup guide that came with it: night lights down the hallway, and her bowl and box where she can always see them. So I can't tell you which part did what. I can only tell you what I wrote down. Week 1. About half a milliliter in her wet food each evening. She ate every bite. After months of capsule wars, I nearly cried over a clean bowl. Lost moments that week: 11. Came when called: once. Week 2. Nothing I could swear to. Then on Friday she walked to her box on her own, twice, with no standing and staring. I drew two stars in the margin. Week 3. I was brushing her on the couch and heard a sound I hadn't heard since Christmas. A purr, small and rusty. I didn't move until it stopped. Week 4. A bad week. A thunderstorm, two lost nights, and a morning she stared at the closet door for most of an hour. I almost stopped writing. Week 6. I came home after three days at my daughter's. The last time I'd been away, Hazel had hidden under the guest bed and flinched when I reached for her. This time she was on my pillow. She lifted her head, looked at me for a second, and trotted down the hallway chirping. It was the little chirp she used to make when I came home from work. I sat down on the hallway floor with her and cried like an idiot. Week 8. I compared the first page with the last. Lost moments: from 11 a week to 4. Came when called: from 1 day in 7 to 5. She isn't a young cat again. She still has foggy afternoons. But I have more of her than I had in the winter. More hours when she's Hazel. I never signed the MRI form. My vet and I agreed to revisit it if anything new showed up: a seizure, circling, a head tilt, sudden blindness. I stopped paying for answers that only said "old." I put the journal in my purse for her next checkup, so my vet can see what I see. And when my brother asked again whether it was time, I told him the truth. "Not yet. When it is, I'll know, and I'll choose it out of love. But it won't be because of a shrug." My friend Ruth and I met in a caregivers' group, the year both our mothers were in memory care. Her cat Oscar is 18. Last month she texted me a photo of him staring at the wall, with one line: "Is this what Mom did?" I sent her my whole folder. The Edinburgh study, the blood pressure question, the Supporting-the-Old Pill. She called her vet first. Oscar's blood pressure turned out to be high, and he's on medication for it now. Then she added the drops to his dinner as well. Last week she wrote: "He came and found me in the garden. On his own." If you take one thing from my story, take these three questions. 1. Has anyone checked what can be fixed? Ask for these by name: blood pressure and eyes, thyroid, hearing, pain and arthritis, kidneys. If you see sudden new signs (a seizure, circling, a head tilt, sudden blindness, a cat who stops eating), see your vet this week. 2. Once those are checked, what is anyone doing for her brain? Not her kidneys. Not her sleep. Her brain. If the answer is "nothing, she's old," you aren't crazy for wanting more. 3. Is she still in there? If she still has good hours, if she still comes back when you say her name, then there's still a map to support. Researchers keep finding that earlier is better. "She's just old" isn't a diagnosis. It's an observation. If you've stood in a doorway watching her cry in a room she's known her whole life... If you've caught yourself asking, "I did feed you, right?"... If she's looked at you, just for a second, like she didn't know you... She hasn't stopped loving you. Her map is fading. And you're allowed to help her hold on to it.
headline: She Hadn’t Stopped Loving Me. Her Map Was Fading.

adCopy: Our rescue's intake director dropped off a litter of four at my house in April. She got as far as the kitchen, stopped, and asked me how many cats I had in the house at that moment. I said nine. She said that isn't possible. My name is Rhonda Beck. I'm 49, I live outside Akron, and I've been a foster for the same cat rescue for eleven years. Three hundred and forty kittens have come through my house. Bottle babies in the spare bedroom. Weaned litters in the sunroom. Whatever the shelter can't hold that week goes wherever I have floor space. Four litter boxes in a 1,600 square foot house. I have scrubbed more litter pans than anybody I know. And last spring I was about two months from telling the rescue I was done. Not because of the work. The work I can do. Because of the smell, and because of what the smell was costing the kittens. adCopy: I came home to my cat licking the shower floor. In Phoenix. In July. His fountain pump had been dead for 9 hours. It was the 3rd pump to die in 14 months. All 3 died the same way. My dad cleaned pools for 31 years. He figured out why in about 10 seconds. I'm Jessica. I'm 44. I live in Phoenix with Otis, a 12-year-old gray cat who will not drink still water. He never has. Put a full bowl in front of him and he stares at it like it insulted him. He drinks from faucets, and he drinks from his fountain. That's why the fountain matters in this house. And if you live anywhere with hard water, you already know what I'm about to describe. A white crusty ring on the spout within a week. A chalky line around the bowl. And then, a few months in, the rattle. I did everything I was supposed to. Scrubbed it every Sunday. Changed the filters. Soaked the bowl in vinegar once a month to get the white stuff off. Pump number 1 rattled for a week, hummed for a day, and quit. Month 5. I bought another one. $14.99. Pump number 2 did the exact same thing. Month 10. Another $14.99. I put the dead ones on a shelf in the garage. I don't know why. Then July. It was 114 degrees that day. I was grabbing my keys at 7:40 in the morning when I heard pump number 3 rattle and go quiet. I was late. The bowl was full. I told myself he'd be fine until tonight. I got home at 4:50. The fountain was full. He hadn't touched it. Otis was in my bathroom, licking the floor of the shower around the drain. I turned on the faucet and he drank for 2 minutes without stopping. I sat on the edge of the tub and felt like the worst person in Arizona. That Saturday my dad came over. I showed him the shelf. 3 dead pumps in a row. He picked up the newest one and popped the front off with his thumb. I didn't know it came off. There's a tiny magnet inside that spins. It was crusted in white, like chalk. And packed over the chalk, a layer of pink-brown slime. "That's calcium," he said. "And the slime's living on it. Slime loves a rough surface. Same as a pool wall." Then he asked me the question. "When you clean this thing, do you ever clean in here?" No. I cleaned what I could see. He explained it the way he used to explain it to customers. The water in a fountain doesn't sit in the bowl. It gets pulled into the pump, spun past that magnet, pushed up a tube, and out the spout. Every sip Otis takes has made that trip. The white ring on the spout is just the part that shows. The same crust is building inside the pump, where the gaps are too tight for a brush. A little more every week. Until one morning the magnet can't turn. That's the rattle. That's the hum. That's the quiet. I looked it up later. The fountain company's own troubleshooting page says hard water deposits can stop the impeller from turning. They know. So every Sunday I scrubbed the bowl, and every Sunday the clean water went straight through a crusty, slimy pump and back out to my cat. "You were brushing the tile and ignoring the plumbing," my dad said. "Looks great. Pump still dies." I asked him if I had to take the pump apart every week now. "In 31 years I never took a pool's plumbing apart to clean it. You can't scrub a pipe. You put the treatment in the water and let the pump carry it through." "That fountain is a very small pool. It has its own pump. Use it." A tiny version of the same idea. Put something that fizzes in the water, leave the pump running, and it pulls the cleaner through its own route. Intake, magnet, tube, spout. Over and over. I said I'd just run vinegar through it. He made a face. Vinegar is fine on crust, he said, but it does nothing much for slime, and the whole house smells like a pickle jar. I knew that part. Otis avoids the bowl for a day every time I use it. "And do not put anything from my truck in there," he said. "He drinks out of this." He gave me 3 rules. Made for pet bowls and fountains. Not pools. Not coffee makers. Not dentures. A short ingredient list you can read. No bleach. It runs through the pump, then rinses all the way out before he drinks. I asked on Nextdoor, because everybody on my street has the same water. A woman 2 blocks over answered. "I use the Nordly Labs ones. They're made for bowls and fountains." I checked their page against my dad's 3 rules. Made for pet bowls. A short ingredient list in plain English. One of them is citric acid, the same stuff that makes lemons sour, and it's there to dissolve the white hard-water ring. And the directions say to drop one in, let the pump run about 15 minutes, then drain and rinse well before you refill. $29 for 10 tablets. $2.90 a clean. Pump number 4 was about to make it $44.97 in replacement pumps. But I wasn't doing pump math anymore. I was doing the math on a 12-year-old cat, 114 degrees, and 9 hours with nothing he'd drink. Our vet has told me twice that older cats who don't drink enough are the ones she sees for UTIs and kidney trouble. I thought about that on the edge of the tub. I ordered them that night, with pump number 4. First Sunday, I dropped a tablet in with the pump running and let it fizz for 15 minutes. Drained it. Rinsed it 3 times. Refilled it. The white ring on the spout had gone soft. Most of it wiped off with my thumb. After the second Sunday it was gone. That was 10 weeks ago. Sunday is a tablet, a fizz and a rinse. The crust hasn't come back. I haven't heard the rattle. Pump number 4 is still running, and I check it every morning before I pick up my keys. My dad took 2 tablets home for his dog's water bowl. He calls it "shocking a very small pool." If you've got a white crusty ring on your cat's fountain right now. If you've already replaced a pump, or 2, or 3. If yours is rattling as you read this. That rattle is the warning I walked past on my way out the door. It's not you. It's your water, and a part of the fountain nobody told you to clean. They're called Water Fountain Cleaning Tablets, from Nordly Labs. 👉 https://nordlylabs.com/products/water-bowl-cleaning-tablets They give you 180 days. Even if you use every tablet and you're not happy, you email them and get your money back. That's why I tried it. The 3 dead pumps are still on the shelf in my garage. I keep them there on purpose now. Otis hasn't licked a shower floor since. Jessica, 44 Phoenix, AZ

adCopy: I almost bought a 3rd cat fountain. Plastic got slimy. The $59 stainless one got slimy too. A brewery worker stopped me. It took him about 30 seconds, standing at my kitchen counter. If anyone has ever told you to "just get a stainless one," read this before you spend the money. I'm Jessica. I'm 33. I live in Asheville with 2 cats, Mabel and Gus. Fountain number 1 was a $34 plastic one. I did everything you're supposed to do. Rinsed it every other day. Scrubbed it every Sunday with dish soap. Changed the filter on schedule. By Wednesday the bowl had that slick film. By the weekend, a pink ring around the edge. 14 months of that. So I asked the internet. And the internet had one answer. "Plastic holds bacteria." "Plastic scratches. Get stainless." "We switched to steel and never looked back." That made sense to me. I bought a fountain to give my cats clean water, and apparently I bought the wrong material. So fountain number 2 was stainless steel. $59. The plastic one went on a shelf in the garage. Day 1, it was beautiful. Day 4, I ran my finger along the inside of the bowl. Slick. Day 6, the pink ring was back. On brand-new steel. I stood there doing the math. $34 plus $59. That's $93 on fountains, and the same slime on both. So I did what any reasonable person does. I put a $72 ceramic one in my cart. That Sunday my sister and her husband came over for dinner. Danny works in the cellar at a brewery on the South Slope. His whole job is tanks, hoses and pumps. I was showing my sister the ceramic fountain on my phone when Danny picked the steel one up off the floor. He unplugged it, pulled the pump out of the bottom and held it up. "What's this part made of?" Plastic. "Where's the old fountain?" He came back from the garage with the pump out of that one too. He set them side by side on my counter. Different brands. Basically the same little black pump. "You didn't buy a new fountain," he said. "You bought a new bowl." Then he popped the cover off the steel fountain's pump with his thumbnail. I did not know it came off. There's a tiny magnet in there called an impeller. It was wrapped in pink-brown slime. On a fountain I had owned for 3 weeks. Danny explained it like I was a new hire. The water doesn't just sit in the bowl. It gets pulled into the pump, spun past that magnet, pushed up a tube, and out the spout. Every sip Mabel and Gus take has made that trip. That route is dark and wet, and the gaps are too tight for a brush. That's where the slime lives. The film in the bowl is only the part you can see. So I'd scrub the bowl, refill it, and plug it in. And the first thing the clean water did was run through the one part I never cleaned, and carry the old gunk right back out. "It's like pouring beer through a dirty tap line into a clean glass," he said. "Doesn't matter how nice the glass is." The slime didn't grow back from nothing. It got a head start. Plastic bowl. Steel bowl. The $72 ceramic bowl in my cart. Every one of them changes the glass. None of them touch the line. The part that made me mad came later. I looked up the instructions for both fountains. Both say to take the pump apart and clean inside it every 2 weeks. It's in there. Nobody reads it. I'd owned 2 fountains and never knew the pump opened. I asked Danny if I was supposed to do that with Q-tips every week for the rest of my life. He laughed. "We don't take the lines apart at work. Breweries quit doing that back in the 1950s. You run the cleaner through the same route the beer takes, and the pump does the work." "Your fountain already has a pump. It's a tiny version of the same setup." Put something that fizzes in the water, leave the pump running, and it pulls the cleaner through its own route. Intake, impeller, tube, spout. Over and over. I had a box of coffee maker descaler tablets under the sink. They fizz. I was halfway to the fountain with one when Danny took the box and read the back. "This is made for a coffee machine. I wouldn't put my cleaner from work in there either. They drink out of this." He gave me 3 rules. Same 3 he uses at work. Made for the job. Pet bowls and fountains, not coffee makers or dentures. You can read what's in it. Short list, no bleach. It rinses all the way out before anybody drinks. I found it in a Reddit thread about pink slime. Somebody wrote, "I use the Nordly Labs ones. They're made for bowls and fountains." I checked all 3 rules against their page. Made for pet bowls. A short ingredient list in plain English, things like citric acid and baking soda. And the directions say to drop one in, let the pump run about 15 minutes, then drain and rinse well before you refill. $29 for 10 tablets. That's $2.90 a clean. The ceramic fountain in my cart was $72. That's about 6 months of weekly cleans. I deleted the fountain and ordered the tablets. First Sunday, I dropped one in with the pump running and let it fizz for 15 minutes. Drained it. Rinsed it 3 times. Refilled it. Day 4, I ran my finger along the inside of the bowl. Smooth. That was 2 months ago. Sunday is now a tablet, a fizz and a rinse. I still change the water in between, because slime always tries to come back. It just doesn't get a head start anymore. And the $34 plastic fountain is out of the garage. I ran a tablet through it and put it upstairs by the bedroom. It stays as clean as the steel one. It was never the plastic. A woman at work told me last week she was about to order a stainless fountain because hers keeps getting slimy. I said, "Open the pump first." She texted me that night. A photo of her impeller and one word. "WHAT." If you've scrubbed the bowl on Sunday and felt the film by Wednesday. If somebody told you plastic was the problem and you believed them like I did. If you have a nicer fountain sitting in your cart right now. You're not doing it wrong. You were handed a problem with a piece missing. Here's what still bugs me. I bought the steel one because I didn't want my cats drinking bacteria. That was the whole point of the $59. And the entire time, their water was running through a pump packed with the exact buildup I was paying to get away from. I don't know what years of that does to a cat. I'm not a vet. I just know it's the reason I spent the money in the first place. So here are your 3 options. Buy another fountain. It comes with the same kind of pump. Take the pump apart with Q-tips every week. It works. It's 30 minutes of your Sunday. Or drop a tablet in and let the pump clean its own route for 15 minutes. They're called Water Fountain Cleaning Tablets, from Nordly Labs. 👉 https://nordlylabs.com/products/water-bowl-cleaning-tablets They give you 180 days. Even if you use every tablet and you're not happy, you email them and get your money back. After $93 in fountains, that's why I tried it. I never bought the 3rd fountain. Jessica, 33 Asheville, NC

A guest's 1 star review shut down our farm Airbnb for 3 weeks this past spring. Then 2 months later the same woman who nearly ruined our business called me looking for forgiveness. I wasn't ready to give it to her. But when she told me what happened I ended up on my kitchen floor crying. This is going to sound like I'm crazy but I promise you every word of it happened. Let me give you a bit of backstory behind our farm. Walt and I have a small cattle farm about 40 minutes outside of Ashland. Cattle, a few goats, chickens that do whatever they want. We have been out here going on 30 years now. When our boys left for college and never came back, we turned their bedrooms into a little farm stay on Airbnb. That has been our side income for about 9 years now. It didn't make us millions. But it made enough to cover about half the mortgage on a farm that doesn't exactly print money on its own. People drive up from the city to sit on our porch and watch the cows and hear what quiet sounds like. They pet the goats and take pictures of the chickens and go home talking about how they want to move to the country. They never do. But they come back, and that's fine by us. I have always wanted our guests to feel like they're coming to stay with family, not checking into some hotel. So from day 1 I have been leaving a little welcome basket on the kitchen counter. The kind of thing you would find at your grandmother's house, if your grandmother lived on a farm. Honey from the apiary down the road. A loaf of caraway bread the Amish girls bake fresh on Tuesdays. A round of cottage cheese from the Petersens. And tucked in the back behind the honey, a small amber bottle of drops that my neighbor Margaret has been giving me for years. She makes them herself from plants she grows. She presses the oil and bottles it by hand, and when you open the bottle it smells faintly of clove and something green. She told me to set some out for guests. So I did. I never really thought much about it. I never asked what was in it. Margaret said it was good for people, and I have trusted Margaret about everything since we moved out here. So I put it in the basket the same way I put in the honey. Now here's a thing about that bottle you need to know, because the whole story turns on it. In 9 years and over 400 guests, I can count on 1 hand the people who ever opened it. It has no label. It looks like something you would ask about first. And nobody ever asked. Guests ate the bread and took the honey home, and the little amber bottle sat behind the honey and came back to me full, or near enough. Every time. Until Diane P. booked a weekend, because her grandkids live about an hour from here and she wanted somewhere quiet to stay while she visited them. Diane told me later why she opened it. When she twisted the cap off, it smelled like clove. Her mother used to keep clove oil in the cupboard. She figured it was some local thing we made, set out with the honey and the bread, the way people out here do. So that first morning she put a few drops in her coffee, and gave Don his. They never made it to the grandkids. They left Sunday morning without saying goodbye. I always hear guests leave. I hear the car doors and I come out and wave and say come back anytime. That's just what I do. I have done it for over 400 guests. Sunday morning I heard the doors and the engine and the gravel. By the time I got to the porch they were already gone. No wave. No goodbye. Just the key on the counter and 2 sets of sheets that needed stripping. I knew something was wrong. I didn't know what until I saw the review she had posted within the hour. ⭐ (1/5) "We were visiting family in the area and booked this farm stay for the weekend because the photos looked nice and peaceful. The property is beautiful and the hosts are very sweet people. There was a welcome basket on the counter which was a nice touch. But there was a small unlabeled bottle of drops in the basket and we both tried some thinking it was like a local herbal thing, and by Saturday we were both violently sick. Stomach cramps and in and out of the bathroom all Saturday night, the both of us. I'm not saying they put it there on purpose but I do think it's irresponsible to leave unlabeled drops in a guest basket without any kind of explanation of what it is. We came up here to visit our grandchildren and we were too sick to go see them. Very disappointing. Wouldn't book again." I read that standing in the kitchen with my coffee going cold in my hand. 9 years of hosting and not 1 single complaint. And now this woman is telling the internet we poisoned her on a weekend she came up to see her grandkids. And there was 1 more thing, which I didn't find until I went to reset the basket for the next guests. The little amber bottle was gone. Sheets, towels, key. Everything else right where it belonged. The bottle had left in their car. I stood there looking at the empty spot behind the honey, and a cold thought walked through me. She thinks it made her sick, and she took it with her. People don't pack up a thing they hate unless they mean to hand it to somebody. A lab. A lawyer. Somebody. 3 days later I got an email from Airbnb saying a guest had reported a health and safety concern at our farm stay, and our listing was under review and could be permanently removed from the platform. 9 years. Over 400 guests. Half the mortgage on a farm that doesn't make money on its own. All of it about to disappear because of a bottle of drops in a welcome basket that I put there because I wanted guests to feel at home. I wrote back that same night. I told them it was a local herbal product from my neighbor down the road. I told them it wasn't a medication. I told them I had been putting it in that basket for 9 years and no guest had ever had a problem. They pulled the listing the next morning. Under review pending investigation. That first week I did the only thing I could think to do. I printed the email, and Diane's review with it, and walked the quarter mile down to Margaret's. She read it on her porch, handed it back, and said, "It's plants, Rachel. It has never hurt a soul in 40 years. Tell them that." "That's all you're going to give me?" "That's all you asked for." I want you to remember that answer, because I didn't understand it until June. I walked home half mad at her. I was fighting for my listing. I wasn't looking for an education. So I didn't get one. For 3 weeks our farm stay was off the platform. No bookings and no income. Walt and I sat at the kitchen table that first night and just looked at each other, because neither one of us knew what to say. Thank the Lord they put us back up at the end of the month. They said they weren't going to remove us permanently. But the review would stay. And they recommended I reconsider including ingestible products in guest amenities. But the damage was done. That 1 star sat at the top of our listing like a warning sign. 2 cancellations came in May. People would book, read the reviews, and cancel. I watched it happen twice, and both times I knew exactly why. Walt didn't say a word about any of it. But I saw him looking at the listing on his phone 1 night. He just closed it and put the phone down on the arm of the chair. And that was worse than anything he could have said. I thought about calling Diane probably 100 times. I typed out a response to her review twice and deleted it both times. Because anything I wrote just sounded like I was making excuses for making somebody sick on our farm. Margaret hands me a fresh bottle every month or so. For 9 years I had tucked each one into the basket without a thought. The first morning I went to set the new one out, I stood there holding it for a long time. The last one had nearly ended us. And the last one was out there somewhere, in that woman's house, waiting to become whatever she meant it to become. I couldn't do it. For the first time in 9 years, the basket went out without it. I put Margaret's fresh bottle in the junk drawer, under the rubber bands and the dead batteries, and I closed it. I didn't tell Margaret. I didn't tell Walt. But every time I opened that drawer for a twist tie, it was in there. Looking at me. Then in June my phone rang. Number I didn't recognize. I almost let it go to voicemail. "Rachel? This is Diane. I stayed at your farm back in April." Of course I knew exactly who she was. She was the reason we almost lost everything. She wasn't angry. That was the first thing I noticed. Back in April she was angry. On this call she was something else. Scared and sorry and confused all at the same time. And it came out as crying. "Rachel, I know I have no right to call you after what I did to your listing. I have been trying to get Airbnb to take that review down for 3 weeks. I have called them 4 times. They keep telling me the editing window closed and there's nothing they can do. I don't think they're going to remove it. "And the review isn't even the thing I'm most ashamed of. That Monday morning, I had the health department's number pulled up on my phone and half a complaint written out on a notepad. An official report, Rachel. The kind a farm stay doesn't come back from. "Don is the one who made me wait a day. "If Monday night hadn't happened, you would have gotten an inspector instead of this phone call. "And I have to be honest about why it took me 2 months to dial your number. I told myself I couldn't call you until I had fixed what I broke. That's why I spent 3 weeks on the phone with Airbnb. I wanted to come to you with that review already gone. "I failed. So here I am calling you anyway, with the review still up, and about a week left in the bottle. Because I have run out of pride before I run out of drops. "I owe you an explanation and I owe you an apology. And honestly I don't know which one to start with." I didn't say anything. I just held the phone. "Rachel, I need to tell you what happened after we left your farm. Because something happened that I can't explain. And I have spent 2 months trying to make sense of it on my own, and I can't do it anymore. "That first morning we both put a few drops in our coffee. Don's legs were sore from the drive and I had a headache, and we thought it was some local herbal thing, like the honey. So I put a few drops in my coffee and gave him his. "Don took his and said, well, that came back up on me a little, tastes like clove. And that was the whole event. We went out and looked at the cows. "Nothing happened that day. Nothing the next morning either. It was just a nice little thing we did with our coffee, like the bread and the honey. "The grandkids had school Friday. So the plan was the farm to ourselves that day, and then the grandchildren all weekend. The ballgame Saturday. Sunday lunch. "Friday morning we took a few more drops each, the way you finish what a host leaves out for you. I'd have felt rude not to. "Saturday it turned. The cramps came on by the afternoon, and we told ourselves we had caught a bug. You know how you do. We called the kids, canceled the ballgame, said we would be there for Sunday lunch instead. We took it easy and waited for it to pass. Because that's what a bug is. Something you wait out. "It didn't pass. Saturday night was the bathroom, all night, the both of us. "And 1 of them doesn't grow in Ohio dirt, and I'll not stand in my own garden and pretend it does. The clove comes in whole, never powdered, and I press it here myself. "Clove is the lock on the nursery door. One of the only things on God's earth that gets through the coating on the eggs. Without it, every cleanse you ever heard of starts over at week 3, when the eggs hatch into an empty house." Then she stopped at the end of the row and turned around. "And the last thing in that bottle doesn't grow anywhere. It's not a plant at all. "When they finally let go of you, they leave a wall behind them that's been chewed on for years. You have to rebuild it or you'll just be handing the next lot a soft place to anchor. "So there's a thing in there called fulvic acid, and all it does is patch the wall. It doesn't kill anything. It's the part that makes it stay done." 6 things. 4 problems. Kill and flush in 1 bottle. "And then twice a year after that, spring and fall, same as you would any animal that walks on dirt," Margaret said, and nodded toward my pasture. "The dirt doesn't quit, Rachel. So neither do we. That's the part that answers your friend's question. The one she's scared to ask. It's not that it stops working. It's that the world doesn't stop being the world." "That's what has been in your basket for 9 years, Rachel. And you have been handing it to 400 strangers and never once took it seriously yourself." I didn't say anything. Because she was right, and there was nothing to say. Then I asked her the practical question. Because half the mortgage on our farm had already been threatened by that bottle, and I wanted to know exactly what I was dealing with. "Margaret. Who else gets this? Besides my basket and the families on this road?" "My granddaughter makes it now," she said. "Has for a few years. I got too old to keep up with the asking, and folks started coming from too far away. "She grows from my seed. Presses the oils cold and seals them the same week they come out of the ground, so nothing sits around going flat. Small batches. Same rules I used. The only thing that changed is whose hands do the lifting. "She calls it Wild Harvest. Her name for it, not mine." And then she gave the 3 of us the same speech I have since learned she gives everybody, instead of a sales pitch. "Whatever you take, mine or anybody's, you check it against 4 things. "It names all 6. Not wormwood and a maybe. If a label can't tell you what handles the eggs, it doesn't handle the eggs, and you're buying week 3 all over again. "The dose is a real dose. Mine runs about 6,600 milligrams' worth of the 4 big ones in a day's serving. A pinch on a label is there to be printed, not to be taken. "It goes in as oil, not dust. What's inside mine is pressed liquid, sealed away from the air. Half of what's sold as an herb capsule is a dry ground leaf that lost its oils on a warehouse shelf a year ago. Cooked plants are dead plants. "And the fourth one, the bottle will tell you itself. Put a drop on your tongue. If you can feel the herbs come through, the oils are alive. If nothing comes through, you bought colored water. "If it can't pass those 4, it's dust in a bottle. I don't care whose name is on it. Mine included. Run the test on mine too." Diane ordered from the granddaughter's website from Margaret's porch, before we had even walked back up the road. I didn't. And I want to tell you why, because it matters. I had quit that bottle twice on day 2. I had spent 9 years not asking 1 question about it. I was done taking things on trust. Even Margaret's. So that night I sat at my kitchen table with the website open and read that label the way I read a feed label before I buy a mineral block. Slow. Twice. All 6 named. 6,600 milligrams' worth in the daily serving. Oil in a sealed bottle, not powder. 3 of her 4 things, right there in print. Then I ordered. Because the fourth thing you can't read. The fourth thing you have to feel. The bottle came, and I ran Margaret's test on it before I did anything else. I put a drop on my tongue over the sink. Clove first. Then the warmth of the herbs underneath, coming through about 3 seconds later. 4 for 4. Margaret says the clove is her grandmother's oldest trick, because nobody keeps taking what they can't stand. And the herbs are the test. If nothing comes through behind the clove, the oils died on a shelf somewhere and the eggs will win. The clove is the welcome. The herbs underneath are the medicine. That morning I started it proper. A full dropper before breakfast, before anything else went down, the way the label says. No more half measures, and no more quitting. Days 2 and 3 were rough. Same as before. Same as always. Bathroom. Headache. That heavy feeling. But this time I knew what it was. This time a woman had spent 2 hours telling me exactly what was leaving and why it fights on the way out. So I drank my water and I kept going. And yes. I saw things leave me too, same as Diane. I'm not going to describe it. You already know. But I stood in my own bathroom at 66 years old, looking down at the reason 14 years of doctors found nothing wrong with me. Day 4, something shifted. Like somebody opened a window in a room that had been sealed for 14 years. Week 2, the bloating was gone. I looked down at my stomach at 7 in the evening and it was flat. I just stood there in the kitchen looking at it. And the 4 o'clock thing went quiet. I walked past the cabinet and nothing asked me for anything. Both broadcasters off the air at once. Margaret said that's why the craving doesn't fade. It stops. Week 3. The week everything Diane and Don ever bought crashed on them. Monday, nothing. Tuesday, nothing. Wednesday I walked to the barn without stopping, which I hadn't done in 3 years. And that same week I drove to Ashland and back without once running the map of restrooms in my head. If you keep that map too, you know exactly what I'm telling you. The clove reached the eggs. The wormwood broke the shield. The pumpkin seed swept the dead out clean. Nothing left standing to start it over. Week 4, I remembered where I put the good shears, and my neighbor's phone number. And the word I had been losing mid sentence for 3 years was just there again. Like it never left. Week 6, down 9 pounds without changing 1 thing on purpose. Which sounds like a lot until you do the math on a woman who quit eating half a jar of honey standing at the sink every single afternoon for 14 years. That's where it came from. The 4 o'clock stopped, so the extra stopped with it. And sleeping through the night. Through it. Week 8, I went to the doctor. The same doctor who told me for years it was my age. He ran the bloodwork, looked at the screen for a long time. Then at me. Then back at the screen. "Your B12 is in normal range. That hasn't been normal since we have been tracking it. Your iron is up. Your markers are down significantly. Whatever you're doing, keep doing it." He didn't ask what. I told him anyway. He wrote something on a notepad. Not on my chart. On his notepad. Week 10, Saturday evening, Walt came up from the barn and found me sitting on the dock. I haven't done that in the evening in 3 years. He stopped on the path and looked at me like he wasn't sure it was me. "You coming or not," I said. He sat down. He took my hand the way he used to. We stayed until the stars came up. That was the best evening I have had in years. And there's 1 more thing I did, the Sunday after my week 3. The week I walked to the barn without stopping. I opened the junk drawer, took Margaret's bottle out from under the rubber bands, and put it back in the basket. Where it had sat for 9 years. Where it will sit from now on. It went out in fear. It came back in certainty. That's the whole distance I traveled, measured in 1 small amber bottle. 3 weeks after that Saturday at Margaret's table, Diane texted me a photo. Don at his workbench. Both hands around a sanding block. Working a piece of wood like the last 4 years never happened. 5 words underneath. "I have my husband back." I printed it. It's on my refrigerator right now. Right next to her 1 star review, which I also printed. Because I want to look at the 2 of them side by side every morning. The worst thing that ever happened to our listing and the best thing that ever happened to the 4 of us. And they're the same bottle. And here's the part I need to say plainly. Because it's the reason I'm writing this at all, and it's bigger than my farm. The CDC estimates over 60 million Americans are carrying a parasite right now. That number has sat on their website for years. Every country on earth except this one runs a deworming program. The WHO deworms over a billion people a year. India deworms its schoolchildren twice a year. We deworm our dogs. Our cats. Our cattle. I deworm 12 head every spring and fall, because they walk on dirt and parasites live in dirt, and not doing it would be negligent. I walked that same dirt for 14 years and never once cleaned myself. Your dog has been cleaned twice a year its whole life. You have never been cleaned once. If your stomach has been bloated every evening for years and your doctor keeps saying it's your age, hear this. The test he used to rule this out catches about 1 in 5. Your negative result didn't mean you were clear. If you have tried the cleanses and the detoxes and nothing ever held past 2 weeks, you weren't failing. The product was incomplete. It did 1 job out of 4, and the eggs hatched into the field you cleared for them. If you stand at your counter at 4 in the afternoon eating something you swore you wouldn't touch, that order was never yours. 2 things that feed on sugar were placing it. When they're gone, it doesn't get quieter. It stops. Mine stopped. Diane's stopped. And if you tried something once, felt terrible for 2 days, and threw the bottle away, you did exactly what I did twice. And what Diane did with a 1 star review. You quit on the bad part right before the good part. https://www.wildrootbotanics.com/products/wildroot-botanics%C2%AE-wormwood-clove-drops-natural-herbal-parasite-cleanser-for-a-cleaner-healthier-gut-v2?view=pdp EDIT: A few things, because my messages filled up and the same questions keep coming. P.S. The guarantee is real. When my first bottle ran out, I ordered 2 more from the granddaughter's website, and the question I sent in got answered by a real person the same afternoon. You can tell the size of an operation by who answers. 30 days, money back. Margaret set that rule herself. If it doesn't work for somebody, she doesn't want their money. I gave 14 years of copays to people who never once offered me a dime back for a pamphlet that fixed nothing. A 79 year old woman with a garden puts her own money behind her work. They never did. P.P.S. About the rough days, because everybody asks. If days 2 and 3 are hard, that's not the plants turning on you. That's the die off. Everything that has been living in you, leaving the only way it can. Diane wrote a 1 star review at the bad part, and missed knowing she was 4 days from the best thing that ever happened to her. Drink your water and get to day 4. That's where it turns. And when you see what leaves, you'll stop wondering forever whether it was all in your head. 2 more things, said plain. Put a drop on your tongue. If you can feel the herbs come through, you have the real thing. If nothing comes through, you bought dust, not plants. And if a doctor has you on medications, you talk to them before you change anything. Margaret says that to every person at her table. The woman who grows the medicine tells you to call your doctor. Let that tell you who she is. P.P.P.S. And if some part of you still thinks parasites are a third world problem, go type 1 word into your search bar tonight. Cyclospora. There's an outbreak of it moving through this country right now, this summer, in grocery store produce. Bagged salads. Raspberries. Fresh basil. Thousands of confirmed cases across dozens of states, part of it traced to lettuce sold at stores you shop at, and the CDC is still hunting clusters they can't explain. I'm not telling you this treats that outbreak. I'm telling you the dirt never quit, and the produce aisle is the proof. 1 parasite. 1 summer. Your grocery store. P.P.P.P.S. Last thing. Margaret's granddaughter makes it in small batches because Margaret won't let it be made any other way. When a batch is gone, it's gone until the next one is ready. And there's no rushing a 79 year old woman who bottles by hand. I keep a spare in my cabinet at all times, because I spent 9 years with the answer sitting in a basket on my counter, and I'm never going to be caught without it again. If it's in stock today, I'd not assume it stays that way. https://www.wildrootbotanics.com/products/wildroot-botanics%C2%AE-wormwood-clove-drops-natural-herbal-parasite-cleanser-for-a-cleaner-healthier-gut-v2?view=pdp Diane's 1 star review is still on my refrigerator. Right next to Don's photo at the workbench. The review almost ended us. What was in that bottle gave all 4 of us back. Don is in his garage. Walt and I are on the dock. Margaret is on her porch, splitting kindling at 79. And the bottle is back in the basket. With a label on it now, and a little card that says ask me about this one. I pulled it once, in fear, and I understand why I did. But I know what's in it now. I heard it from the woman who grows it, at her own table, with my own ears. We're never pulling it again.

Vancouver is about to get a dog wash with dog beer, dog tequila, salon-quality cologne, a self-serve marketplace, and absolutely nobody standing behind a counter. And somehow, the dog wash might not even be the weirdest part. Theo’s Self Serve Dog Wash is getting very close to opening, and this whole thing has grown into a lot more than just a place to rinse off a muddy dog. The idea from the beginning was simple: make dog washing easier, make the experience better, stay open later, and build something that actually feels useful to local dog owners. So the entire place is self serve. When you walk in, the kiosk is your starting point. You can see how the wash works, check pricing, learn about Theo’s Pack memberships, browse what’s available in the Grab & Go Market, find local dog adventures, discover other pet-friendly businesses through the Blue Tie Network, leave feedback, and figure out what you need without waiting for somebody behind a counter. No appointment required. No awkward scheduling. No trying to convince your dog that Tuesday at 2:15 was somehow the only available option. Come in during open hours, and if the wash is available, you’re good to go. The wash itself is an Evolution self-serve system with shampoo, flea & tick shampoo, conditioner and blow dry included. And if your dog deserves the full spa treatment — or just smells especially questionable — we’ll have Hydra grooming products available in the Grab & Go Market. Hydra is professional salon-quality grooming stuff, and the colognes were one of the easiest decisions we made. They smell ridiculously good. Not “somebody sprayed perfume on a wet dog” good. Actually-good, just-left-the-groomer, why-does-my-dog-smell-better-than-I-do good. We’ll have several scents available, along with premium shampoos and finishing products if you want to upgrade the wash a little. Then there’s the Grab & Go Market. Treats, toys, grooming supplies, drying towels, premium shampoos and colognes, dog drinks, seasonal stuff, things you forgot at home, and things your dog absolutely did not need but somehow talked you into buying anyway. We’re also starting something of our own. Theo’s Treats. We’re starting with simple, high-quality treats like freeze-dried beef lung, but that’s just the beginning. Over time, we want to keep growing Theo’s own lineup with products we actually like and feel good about putting our name on. And yes. There will be dog beer. There will be dog tequila. There will probably be other ridiculous things later because apparently this is who we are now. For people who want even more flexibility, Theo’s Pack members will have extended access from 6 AM–10 PM, while regular walk-in hours will be 8 AM–8 PM. And we’re trying to build something beyond the four walls too. Dog Adventures will help local dog owners find parks, trails, swimming spots, dog-friendly patios and other places around Southwest Washington to explore with their dogs. The Blue Tie Network will help connect people with other great local pet businesses and services. And we’re working toward partnerships with local rescues, foster organizations and community groups so Theo’s can support more than just the dogs walking through the front door. That’s really what Theo’s has turned into. A dog wash, yes. But also a place to discover stuff, find local resources, spoil your dog a little, and hopefully build something useful for the dog community around here. We’re putting the finishing touches on everything now. Opening very soon. So if you’re in Vancouver, Camas, Washougal, Battle Ground, Portland or anywhere nearby with a muddy, hairy, suspiciously smelly dog… Follow the page. Send this to your dog people. And tell us something: What’s one thing you wish a place like Theo’s carried, offered, or did that nobody else around here does? We’re still building this thing. And we’re listening. Theo’s Self Serve Dog Wash 906 SE 164th Ave, Suite 100B Vancouver, WA theosdogwash.com

adCopy: My walking buddy of seven years hired a behaviorist in July. Her dog was put down by Christmas. I'm writing this in my car in the reservoir parking lot at 6:40 on a Sunday morning. For seven years there were two dogs in the back of this car on Sundays. Now there's one. Murphy's orange tennis ball is still in the door pocket where he dropped it on our last Sunday in July, and I can't bring myself to take it out. So if your dog barks, lunges or screams at things, or someone you love has a dog who does, please read this whole thing. I know it's long. I know you've got a dog to walk and a hundred other things to do. But six months ago, I'd have given anything to know what I'm about to tell you, because it would've saved Murphy's life. Seven years ago, the county shelter pulled eleven dogs out of a hoarding house outside Lititz. Two of them were brothers, shepherd-lab mixes, sharing one crate because they wouldn't eat apart. A woman named Ro had already signed the papers for one of them when I walked in. I took the other because I couldn't stand the thought of him going back in that crate alone. We swapped numbers in the parking lot so the boys could still see each other. And every Sunday since, it's been 7am at the reservoir loop. Two thermoses on the same bench. Murphy and Gus wrestling in the wet grass until they were both soaked. Seven years. Through my husband's funeral. Through Ro's hip replacement. We never missed more than a couple of Sundays. Then last May, Ro was walking Murphy down her street when a husky cleared a yard fence and went straight for him. By the time the owner pulled it off, Murphy had a gash across his shoulder that took fourteen stitches. He came home a different dog. Within a month he was lunging at every dog on the street and screaming at the front window. The big goofball who used to flop onto his back for anyone with a free hand went stiff every time a car door slammed. In July, Ro paid $350 for an assessment with a behaviorist. "Severe reactivity," the woman wrote. "Risk of escalation. Strict management, medication, and we'll re-evaluate in three months." Ro called me from the parking lot. I was the first person she told. Not her daughter. Me. "She says I have to change everything, Patty." "What are you going to do?" "Whatever it takes. What else can I do?" She went home and did it all in one afternoon. She put frosted film on the front windows. She called her book club and told them she'd have to sit out for a while. She moved Murphy's walks to 5am, when the street was empty. Then she called me back. "I can't come Sundays anymore," she said. "He can't handle the other dogs at the reservoir. He can't even handle Gus right now." The next Sunday, I walked the loop alone with Gus for the first time in seven years. He kept stopping at the bench and looking back at the parking lot. For the next three months, Ro did every single thing she was told. Prozac every morning, wrapped in a piece of cheese. A $2,800 board-and-train that kept him for two weeks. A forty-minute drive twice a week to a rented field so he could run without seeing another dog. Calming chews from the pet store in a jar by the back door. She skipped her granddaughter's fifth birthday party. She stopped going to church. She couldn't leave him alone for two hours, and she couldn't take him anywhere there were people. The behaviorist had her keep a log in a spiral notebook on the kitchen counter. Every bark at the window, every lunge on the leash got a tally mark and the time. The first week, there were forty-one. I'd sit at her kitchen table and watch her add a mark in the middle of our conversation, and she'd say, "It's okay. It's going to work. It has to work." The re-evaluation was October 9th. Thirty-eight. She sat in the behaviorist's parking lot for forty minutes before she could drive home. Then she called me, crying so hard I thought someone had died. "Patty, I've given up everything. Everything. And it hasn't worked." I told her to give it time. I told her the behaviorist said these things can take six months. I told her Thanksgiving was only a few weeks away, and being around her family would do her good. I've hated myself for saying that every single day since. Thanksgiving was at Ro's sister's house in Ephrata. Ro almost didn't go. She couldn't leave him home alone all day, so she brought him and kept him in his crate in the back bedroom with the door shut, exactly like the behaviorist said. She even taped a sign on the door. Please don't open. Dog sleeping. Ro's brother-in-law Gary was there. Every family has one. Loud, three beers in before the turkey was carved, and always the one at the table saying that dog just needs a firm hand. Ro told him twice to leave Murphy alone. Somewhere between the turkey and the pie, Gary decided he'd show everyone the dog was fine. He walked into the back bedroom, opened the crate and grabbed Murphy by the collar to drag him out. Murphy had been asleep. He bit Gary's forearm. Eleven stitches. By the time I got to the ER, Ro was sitting in the hallway with her coat still on and Murphy's leash wrapped around her hand. Gary reported him to the county before his stitches were even in. When the animal control truck pulled into her driveway the next morning, Ro was waiting outside in her slippers. She had the behaviorist's report, the vet records and the muzzle in her arms. She begged them to let her keep him quarantined at home. She said she'd sign anything, pay anything. They took him anyway. Ten days of bite quarantine at the county shelter. The same building where Ro and I met seven years earlier. I drove her there every single day. We weren't allowed inside, so we sat on a bench by the chain-link fence where she could see his run. On day four, Ro asked one of the kennel attendants how Murphy was doing. He hesitated. "He lies down. Closes his eyes. Looks dead to the world. But he's up every time a door clanks, and then he paces. All night. I don't think he's really slept since he got here." I didn't know then that it was the most important thing anyone would say to us. On day six, Ro called his name through the fence. He looked right at her, and then right through her, like he was trying to place where he'd seen her before. She didn't make a sound until we got back to the car. Then she put her forehead on the dashboard and sobbed. On day nine, there was a hearing. A county officer read the report out loud. Bite to an adult male. And then, "previous attack history." The husky. The dog who came over a fence and tore his shoulder open. They counted that against Murphy. Gary sat at the back of the room and never once looked at us. Day ten. December 6th. 9:15 in the morning. Ro held him on the floor of a small room with a blanket she'd brought from home. He put his head in her lap, the way he did on her couch every night. She told him he was a good boy. She told him over and over, until the vet nodded. I drove her home afterward. The Prozac was on the windowsill above her kitchen sink. The muzzle was hanging by the back door. And the spiral notebook was on the counter, open to the last page. The last tally mark was from Thanksgiving morning. And his tennis ball was still in my car door. I haven't moved it. After December 6th, Ro stopped answering her phone. She didn't go back to church or book club. I'd hoped that once she didn't have Murphy to protect, she might come back to Sundays. She never did. Her daughter told me Ro spent most afternoons in the back bedroom, sitting next to Murphy's empty crate. She hadn't taken it down. She couldn't. Seven years of friendship, and it just went quiet. I kept walking our loop every Sunday with Gus. Just the two of us. And then, in January, Gus started. It was small at first. A bark at the window when the mailman came. Then a growl at a dog across the street. Then a lunge so hard on the leash that I went down on one knee on the ice. In seven years, Gus had never growled at anything. Not the mailman. Not the vacuum. Not even the cat next door. But he'd lost his brother. And somewhere in that, something in him had changed. I knew exactly where this went. I'd watched every step of it from Ro's kitchen table. The tally marks. The 5am walks. The hearing. And every night, the reactive dog groups on Facebook were full of the same posts. "Behaviorist says we're making progress." "Started Prozac this week, fingers crossed." I knew how those stories would end. So I started reading. Every night at the kitchen table, with Gus on the rug by my feet. Vet articles I could barely follow. Shelter websites. Forums at two in the morning. And one thing kept coming up that nobody ever told Ro. Every time a dog like Murphy sees a trigger, his body floods with cortisol, the stress hormone. It should only take a couple of days to come back down. Except with reactive dogs it never gets those days, because the next trigger is only ever a few hours away. For Murphy, it started with the husky. For Gus, it was losing his brother. For some dogs, there's no big moment at all, just one stressful thing piling on top of the next. And this is the part that broke my heart. With that much cortisol in him, his body is so on edge it physically can't let go long enough to get the deep sleep he needs to stay calm around the things that set him off. Think about the worst night's sleep you've ever had. The short fuse the next day. Now imagine that every night for months, with no way of telling anyone. I remember thinking, but Gus sleeps all day. He was out like a light on the rug right then. And then I thought about what that kennel attendant said about Murphy. Looks dead to the world. Up every time a door clanks. You can't tell by looking. A dog can lie there with his eyes shut for hours and never really get the deep sleep his brain needs. And a brain that exhausted can't hold onto anything. That's why Murphy's training never stuck. But this is the part that scares me most. It doesn't stay the same, and it doesn't get better on its own. Every week a dog goes without real rest, he gets a little more exhausted, and it gets a little harder for him to hold himself together. That's exactly what was happening to Murphy the whole time Ro thought she was protecting him. Until a man grabbed his collar while he was sleeping, and he couldn't control what happened next. Everything Ro did, the 5am walks, the frosted windows, giving up Sundays, slowed the damage down. But it never gave back a single night of the sleep he'd already lost. The triggers didn't change. Murphy did. He wasn't dangerous. He wasn't wired wrong. He hadn't really rested since the day that husky came over the fence. The next Sunday, I sat in the reservoir parking lot with the engine off, looking at his tennis ball in my car door. A man with a doodle got out at the far end of the lot, and Gus hit the back window so hard the whole car rocked. I didn't even get out. For the first time in seven years, I didn't walk our loop. I just drove home. The next morning, I took Gus to see our vet of seven years, Dr. Kessler. I told her everything. Murphy. Gus. And everything I'd been reading about cortisol and sleep. Then I asked her about the bottle on Ro's windowsill. "Prozac?" she said. She was quiet for a second. "You're not wrong, Patty. Prozac can turn the volume down on the reaction. Some dogs get trazodone on top to make them drowsy. But neither one gives the brain the deep sleep it's missing. Sedated isn't rested." Sedated isn't rested. I asked her why nobody had ever told Ro that. "Because it's not in the protocol," she said. "Reactivity gets Prozac and a referral to a behaviorist. That's what we're taught. Sleep never really comes up." "Couldn't she have just given him melatonin?" "Some people do," she said. "But melatonin on its own mostly just makes them drowsy. If the cortisol's still sky high, the body won't stay down in deep sleep long enough to matter. You'd have to bring the cortisol down first." I drove from her office straight to the big pet store on Route 30. I stood in the calming aisle for almost an hour. Thundershirts in four sizes. Pheromone collars. CBD oil with a cartoon leaf on the label. Plug-in diffusers. And a whole shelf of calming chews, every bag promising a calmer dog. I bought a bag for $24. It had four and a half stars. I gave Gus one every morning for two weeks. Nothing. Then one night, I actually read the back of the bag. For best results, give 30 minutes before car rides, vet visits or fireworks. Thirty minutes before. They were made to take the edge off for an afternoon. Nothing in that bag ever touched what was happening to him at night. I'd been doing the right thing at the wrong time. And then I remembered the jar of those same chews by Ro's back door, and I had to put the bag down. About three weeks later, a post came up in one of the reactive dog groups. It was from a woman who works at a no-kill shelter outside Columbus. Her shelter had started putting sleep trackers on the dogs' collars. Every dog. Even the ones the staff swore slept like babies. On average, they were getting 48 minutes of deep sleep a night. So a small team of vets donated something to the shelter that lowered the dogs' cortisol AND helped them get the deep sleep they'd been missing. They started giving it to every reactive dog each night, before any training began. Three weeks later, those same dogs were averaging 3 hours and 52 minutes of deep sleep a night.
